en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on the Power of Psychic Faculties.
7. The Question on the Disappearance of the True Dhamma “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Ānanda, the true Dhamma shall now remain for only five hundred years.’”
Furthermore, at the time of his final Nibbāna, when asked a question by the wanderer Subhadda, the Blessed One said:

"If, Subhadda, these bhikkhus were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants. This is a statement that is exhaustive, this is a statement that is complete, this is a statement that is non-figurative.
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was spoken by the Tathāgata—
“If it is said, ‘Ānanda, the true Dhamma will now remain for only five hundred years,’ then the statement that ‘the world will not be empty of arahants’ must be false.

If, however, it was spoken by the Tathāgata that ‘the world will not be empty of arahants,’ then the statement that ‘Ānanda, the true Dhamma will now remain for only five hundred years’ must also be false.”
“This too is a question with two sides, more difficult than the difficult, stronger than the strong, and more knotted than the knotted;
it has come before you. Display therein the expansion of the power of your knowledge, like a sea-monster that has entered within the ocean.
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: ‘Ānanda, the True Dhamma shall now endure for only five hundred years.’”
And at the time of his final Nibbāna, it was said by the Blessed One to the wanderer Subhadda:
“If these monks, Subhadda, were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants.

Now, Great King, that word of the Blessed One has both different meanings and different phrasings: this is the definition of the Dispensation, and this is the elucidation of the practice; thus, those two are far removed from one another.

Just as, Great King, the sky is far removed from the earth, hell is far removed from heaven, the wholesome is far removed from the unwholesome, and happiness is far removed from suffering—even so, Great King, are those two far removed from one another.
Moreover, Great King, let not your question be in vain; I shall explain it to you by bringing them together through their flavor: "The five..."
"Now, Ānanda, when the Blessed One said, 'The true Dhamma shall endure for five hundred years,' he was indicating its exhaustion and thereby delimiting the remainder:
'Ānanda, the true Dhamma would have endured for a thousand years, had the bhikkhunīs not been ordained.
Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma shall endure for only five hundred years.'"
“Great King, when the Blessed One speaks in this way, does he speak of the disappearance of the True Dhamma, or does he reject its realization?
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“Great King, by describing what has been lost and illuminating what remains, he has defined it.”
“Just as, great king, a man who has lost his property might take what remains and announce it to the people, saying: ‘So much of my goods have been lost;

this is what remains,’ even so, great king, the Blessed One, pointing out what was lost, spoke to gods and humans regarding what remained, saying: ‘Ānanda, the true Dhamma shall now endure for only five hundred years.
And as for that which was spoken by the Blessed One—”
‘Ānanda, the true Dhamma will now endure for only five hundred years’—this is a limitation on the teaching.

But when, at the time of his final Nibbāna, he spoke while praising the ascetics to the wanderer Subhadda, saying, ‘If, Subhadda, these bhikkhus were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants’—this was an illustration of the practice. Yet you treat that limitation and that illustration as having a single meaning.
But if you have the desire, I shall speak making it of a single flavor; listen well, attend closely, and be undistracted in mind.
Here, Great King, suppose there were a lake filled with fresh water, bounded and enclosed, being crossed right before one's eyes;
while that lake’s water has not yet been exhausted, a great cloud pours down rain continuously, again and again, upon the surface of the water.
“If it were to rain down, great king, would the water in that pond reach exhaustion and depletion?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“For what reason, great king?”
“Because of the continuous succession of clouds, venerable sir.

“In the same way, Great King, the excellent lake of the True Dharma of the Victor’s teaching—filled with the pure, fresh water of conduct, virtue, qualities, observances, and practice—is standing having risen up and surpassed the peak of existence.
If the sons of the Buddha were to cause the rain-clouds of conduct, virtue, qualities, observances, and practice to fall there again and again, and to pour down upon it, [it would overflow].”
In this way, this excellent pond of the True Dhamma of the Victor’s teaching might endure for a long, extended period;
the world would not be empty of Arahants. It was with reference to this matter that the Blessed One said:
“If, Subhadda, these monks were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants.”
"Furthermore, great king, suppose a great mass of fire were burning and they were to add dry grass, wood, and cow dung from time to time. Would that mass of fire, great king, go out?
"No indeed, venerable sir; rather, that mass of fire would burn more and more, and it would shine more and more.

"In the same way, great king, the excellent teaching of the Conqueror throughout the ten-thousandfold world system burns and shines through the practice of conduct, virtue, qualities, and observances."
But if, Great King, the sons of the Buddha were to strive further, endowed with the five factors of exertion, constantly and heedfully applying themselves;
if, having conceived a desire for the three trainings, they were to train in them;

and if they were to fulfill their conduct and virtue in their entirety—then this excellent teaching of the Conqueror would endure for even longer, for a very long time, and the world would not be empty.
“‘The world would not be empty of Arahants’—it was with reference to this meaning that the Blessed One spoke thus:
‘If, Subhadda, these bhikkhus were to live rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants.

Furthermore, Great King, suppose they were to polish a mirror made of smooth, even, well-wrought, and radiant stainless glass with fine, delicate geruka powder again and again; would then, Great King, dirt, mud, dust, or grime ever arise on that mirror? “No, indeed, Sir.”
“Certainly not, venerable sir; it would only become even more stainless.
“In the same way, Great King, the sublime teaching of the Victor is naturally pure, free from the stains and dust of the defilements.

If the sons of the Buddha [maintain] that sublime teaching of the Victor through their conduct, virtue, qualities, observance of the precepts, practice of austerity, and the quality of ascetic purification...”
"If they were to attend closely, this excellent teaching of the Conqueror would endure for a very long time, and the world would not be empty of Arahants.
It was with reference to this meaning that the Blessed One said:
"If, Subhadda, these monks were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants."
“Great King, the Teacher’s dispensation is rooted in practice; it exists for the sake of practice, remaining as long as practice is not lost.
“Venerable Nāgasena, regarding what you say about ‘the disappearance of the True Dhamma’—what is that disappearance of the True Dhamma?
“Great King, there are these three ways in which the dispensation disappears.”
Which three?
The disappearance of realization, the disappearance of practice, and the disappearance of the signs.

When realization has disappeared, O Great King, even for one who has practiced well, there is no direct penetration of the Dhamma; when practice has disappeared, there is no promulgation of the training rules.
"It disappears; only the mark remains. When the mark has disappeared, there is a severance of the lineage.
These, O Great King, are the three disappearances.

"Well-explained, venerable Nāgasena, is this question! What was profound has been made clear; the knot has been untied. The doctrines of opponents have perished, shattered, and rendered lusterless, for you have assailed the preeminent bull among the leaders of schools."
The seventh question: On the disappearance of the true Dhamma.
